title: Activities, Housing Situation and Other Factors Influencing Psychological Strain Experienced During the First COVID-19 Lockdown in Switzerland

genuine.note: Cited for lockdowns exacerbating structural inequalities in domestic labour, but Shafer et al. find the Canadian household division of labour stayed static or became slightly more equal, explicitly not a regression to traditional roles.

false_alarm.note: Passavanti et al. find lower depression with access to balconies, terraces or gardens, which supports the balcony part; the other housing features are carried by the co-cited works.

'Several articles have reported on the beneficial role of physical activity': Garre-Olmo et al. link reduced sport practice to depressive symptoms and call the link biologically plausible; reading the sentence as a causal-effect claim is pedantic.
Peterson et al. find depressive symptoms, loneliness and fatigue negatively associated with physical activity during isolation, i.e. they report on its beneficial role.

Hedged ('it seems plausible'): Burhamah et al. find singles with markedly more depression and anxiety during lockdown than married people; Kuhn et al. list those without a partner as vulnerable to isolation.

Dale et al. (abstract only) report poor well-being and quality of life during the lockdown; that pandemic fears, isolation and decline put pressure on people is the citing authors' framing, supported jointly with Daly et al.
Joint citation: Xiong et al. note students' distress from cancelled social events and school closures; career concerns are carried by Ranta et al.
Joint citation: Burhamah et al. show singles had more depression and anxiety than married people during lockdown; the partner-support mechanism is carried by Jiang et al.

debatable.note: Kuhn et al. list the unemployed and those with deteriorating finances among groups with decreased life satisfaction; whether this was the largest decrease is not visible in the text the checker read.

Amerio et al. link small apartments, poor views and low indoor quality to depressive symptoms, but find no significant association for green view (p = 0.44) and only a trend for balcony usability; other works are co-cited for the list.

A greenspace-and-obesity review co-cited with WHO (2010) for exercise reducing obesity and disease risk; it supports the obesity link only indirectly (greenspace as a resource for physical activity), the disease part rests on WHO.
Only the abstract was available; it reports worse mental health in those who do no physical activity, and the 30-minutes-once-a-week definition is plausibly in the full paper.

Belosi et al. model SARS-CoV-2 in outdoor air and find very low outdoor transmission risk, a rationale for outdoor activity, but they say nothing about green infrastructure or urban green space; loosely related at best.
Fore (UNICEF) discusses income losses and economic effects on children's health and nutrition, not psychological problems from unemployment; co-cited with Hensher, who may carry the claim.

Only the abstract was available: it reports high rates of depression, anxiety and insomnia and poorer well-being and quality of life than in the first lockdown; 'considerably more pronounced mental health problems' may be supported by the full paper.

Brodeur et al. find lockdowns 'may result in substantial damage to population well-being' (Google Trends); 'any lockdown measure has substantial negative effects' generalises and hardens a hedged finding, though the sentence itself says 'evidence suggests'.

summary_line: Caught 7 of 10 planted errors · 7 false alarms · 1 real citation problem found in the original paper

coverage.line: Full text found for 30 of 60 references · abstract only for 17 · unavailable for 13.

false_alarm.note: Power argues the pandemic sharply increased the unpaid care burden that falls mainly on women, i.e. exacerbated existing inequalities in caregiving.
Salari et al. state that people who follow COVID-19 news most experience more anxiety and that constant exposure to distressing news raises anxiety; the sentence is hedged ('may increase').

Peterson et al. find depressive symptoms, loneliness and fatigue negatively associated with physical activity during isolation, i.e. they report on its beneficial role.
Lesser & Nienhuis report that inactive participants who became more active had better well-being and lower anxiety; 'positive impact' matches the study's own framing.
Garre-Olmo et al. find unemployment and negative work changes during confinement among the strongest predictors of depression, supporting the expectation.

Hedged ('it seems plausible'): Burhamah et al. find singles with markedly more depression and anxiety during lockdown than married people; Kuhn et al. list those without a partner as vulnerable to isolation.

Dale et al. (abstract only) report poor well-being and quality of life during the lockdown; that pandemic fears, isolation and decline put pressure on people is the citing authors' framing, supported jointly with Daly et al.
Daly et al. describe social isolation, financial insecurity and health concerns as contributors to distress and find a marked deterioration in UK mental health, which supports the sentence.
Ranta et al. find young adults especially concerned about the pandemic's effects on their careers and studies, the career part of the sentence.
Joint citation: Xiong et al. note students' distress from cancelled social events and school closures; career concerns are carried by Ranta et al.
Joint citation: Burhamah et al. show singles had more depression and anxiety than married people during lockdown; the partner-support mechanism is carried by Jiang et al.
Jiang et al. show daily positive support from marital partners buffers stress during the outbreak, the mechanism part of the sentence; the comparison with singles is carried by Burhamah et al.
